CLOSED 2026-11-24. No new defect. The investigation independently reproduced the analysis in the pre-existing P1 PKIX-rm8.57, which I did not know about when filing this.

## Answer to this bead's question

The IP-literal bypass found in pkix-aia-http CANNOT occur here, for a structural reason. That bug was that reqwest does not consult a custom DNS resolver when the host is an IP literal, so a RESOLUTION-TIME destination filter is bypassed. pkix-revocation-http has no destination filter at any layer, sync or async. No filter, nothing to bypass.

That is explicit, not an oversight. lib.rs states: "No CDP / AIA URI filtering ... Restrictions on which hosts / schemes are acceptable for revocation fetches ... are a deployment-policy decision and stay outside this crate."

## What I verified rather than assumed

The decision to leave destination policy to the caller is only coherent if the caller's vetting cannot be subverted afterwards. The crate claims exactly that: "the reference clients only follow same-origin redirects by default, so a vetted URL cannot be redirected to a different host behind the caller's back."

That claim holds on BOTH paths:

- clients/reqwest.rs installs same_origin_redirect_policy in new() / try_new(), comparing the preceding URL's origin against the target's and stopping otherwise. This is an active override: reqwest's own default follows up to 10 redirects to ANY origin.
- clients/ureq.rs disables ureq's redirect following entirely and walks same-origin redirects in fetch(), with GET following 301/302/303/307/308 and POST only 307/308 so method and body survive.
- Six tests across tests/review_reqwest_redirect.rs and tests/review_ureq_redirect.rs, all passing. The cross-origin cases mount the internal mock with .expect(0) and call verify(), so they assert the internal server was NEVER CONTACTED rather than merely that an error came back -- the same standard as pkix-aia-http/tests/async_ssrf.rs.

So the redirect asymmetry between the two crates is principled rather than accidental: aia-http refuses redirects outright because it applies its own destination policy that a redirect would escape, while revocation-http permits same-origin redirects because the caller's vetted origin is precisely the boundary being preserved.

## Duplicate of PKIX-rm8.57, which is P1 and open

PKIX-rm8.57 (filed 2026-06-15) covers this and reaches the same conclusion: "This is documented and intentional -- the delegation to the RevocationFetcher trait is the right architecture. But callers may not realize they need to implement host filtering in their RevocationFetcher. A 'Security Considerations' section in the crate rustdoc would help."

I filed this bead without finding that one. Searching beads before filing would have caught it; recording the lapse because it is the second time an existing bead has been missed this session (PKIX-l5ti's reference list was also incomplete).

## What my investigation adds to rm8.57

rm8.57 predates pkix-aia-http's async family, which landed this session under PKIX-j72x. So it could not have noted the cross-crate inconsistency, which is the part worth carrying forward:

Two crates in one workspace now have OPPOSITE defaults for the same threat -- both fetch URLs from a certificate whose signature has not been verified yet.

- pkix-aia-http: default-deny non-public destinations at resolution time, opt-in escape hatch
- pkix-revocation-http: no destination policy, caller vets

Neither is wrong on its own terms, but a consumer who learns that AIA fetching is SSRF-safe by default may reasonably assume revocation fetching is too, and nothing in either crate says otherwise. That strengthens rm8.57's case for a Security Considerations section, and the section should name the contrast with pkix-aia-http explicitly rather than only describing revocation-http in isolation.

Added as a note on rm8.57 rather than kept here.
